topic: Analyse: correlation, regression and root-cause tools

notes.front: What is a scatter plot?
notes.back: A plot of each Y value against its matching X value, used to reveal a relationship or association between two variables.
notes.explanation: The e-Handbook: any non-random structure in the plot is how a relationship between the two variables shows itself.
notes.example: Like a run chart, but the horizontal axis is a second measured variable, such as oven temperature for each batch, instead of time.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.3.26 “Scatter Plot”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: A scatter plot ( Chambers 1983 ) reveals relationships or association between two variables. Such relationships manifest themselves by any non-random structure in the plot.

notes.front: What is the correlation coefficient (Pearson's r)?
notes.back: A measure of the linear correlation between two sets of data, also called Pearson's r.
notes.explanation: It is the covariance of the two variables divided by the product of their standard deviations.
notes.example: Like a slope, but unit-free: r for machine speed and part temperature is the same whether temperature is logged in °C or °F.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Pearson correlation coefficient”, English Wikipedia
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: is a correlation coefficient that measures linear correlation between two sets of data. It is the ratio between the covariance of two variables and the product of their standard deviations

notes.front: What is the coefficient of determination?
notes.back: R²: the proportion of the variation in the dependent variable that is predictable from the independent variable(s).
notes.explanation: It is written R² or r² and said “R squared”; because it is a proportion of variation, it reads as a share of the whole.
notes.example: Like a percentage score for a model: how much of the spread in delivery times the fitted line for distance can account for.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Coefficient of determination”, English Wikipedia
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: the coefficient of determination , denoted R 2 or r 2 and pronounced "R squared", is the proportion of the variation in the dependent variable that is predictable from the independent variable(s).

notes.front: In statistics, what is a residual?
notes.back: The difference between an observed value and the estimated value of the quantity of interest, such as a sample mean.
notes.explanation: Wikipedia notes that the distinction between residuals and errors matters most in regression analysis.
notes.example: A fitted line predicts 42 minutes to pack an order; the order took 45, so its residual is 3 minutes.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Errors and residuals”, English Wikipedia
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: The residual is the difference between the observed value and the estimated value of the quantity of interest (for example, a sample mean ). The distinction is most important in regression analysis

notes.front: What is the least-squares regression line?
notes.back: The straight line that minimises the sum of the squared residuals between the data points and the line.
notes.explanation: Least squares is how simple linear regression defines the “best” fitting line through the data.
notes.example: Like drawing a line by eye through a cloud of points, but with a rule: pick the line whose squared vertical gaps add up to the least.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Simple linear regression”, English Wikipedia, “Fitting the regression line”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: in this article the "best" fit will be understood as in the least-squares approach: a line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals

notes.front: What is multiple regression?
notes.back: A way to model how one continuous process output (Y) depends on several input factors (Xs) together.
notes.explanation: Where simple linear regression has one explanatory variable, multiple regression brings several inputs into one model of a continuous output.
notes.example: Like fitting a line of call length against agent experience, but with queue length and time of day in the same model too.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Multiple Regression”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a multi-vari chart?
notes.back: A graph that splits variation into three families: within a part, between machines or process parts, and over time.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio places it in the Measure and Analyse phases of Six Sigma.
notes.example: Like a run chart of shaft diameters, but each point is grouped by position on the shaft and by lathe as well as by hour.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Multi-vari”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is common cause variation?
notes.back: Variation that is part of the process itself over time, touching every output and everyone who works in the process.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio also labels it “noise”, set against the “signals” of special causes.
notes.example: Small day-to-day wobbles in how long invoices take to approve, with no single event behind them.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Common Cause Variation (Noise)”, p. 3
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is special cause variation?
notes.back: Variation from identifiable factors that make the output non-random; also called assignable or exceptional variation.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio calls such variation “signals”, in contrast to the “noise” of common causes, and sums it up as a few Xs with a big impact.
notes.example: Like everyday noise in invoice times, except one day's invoices all run late because the payment system was down.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Special Cause Variation (Signals)”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the 5 Whys technique?
notes.back: Asking “why?” five times in a row to work down the cause-and-effect chain behind a problem to a root cause.
notes.explanation: Each answer becomes the next question, so the chain follows cause-and-effect links below the first, obvious answer.
notes.example: Like a child's string of “but why?” questions, aimed at one defect and written down as a chain.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional's Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 3: What Is Six Sigma?, “5 Whys Approach”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a cause-and-effect diagram?
notes.back: A fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram: the effect sits at the head and possible causes branch off the spine in groups.
notes.explanation: The guide presents it as a way to spark ideas and keep group brainstorming balanced while people list causes of a problem.
notes.example: A team writes “late deliveries” at the head of the drawing and adds branches for every cause members suggest.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional's Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 3: What Is Six Sigma?, “Cause-and-Effect Diagram”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a Pareto chart?
notes.back: A bar chart of defect or problem types, with the bars sorted from largest to smallest, left to right.
notes.explanation: The guide says this ordering helps teams prioritise which problems to respond to.
notes.example: Like a histogram of complaint types, but sorted so the tallest bar always comes first.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional's Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 3: What Is Six Sigma?, “Pareto Charts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA)?
notes.back: A structured method for finding potential failures in a process or system, and their effects, before any harm occurs.
notes.explanation: The nursing-home guide describes it as a proactive tool: the aim is to remove process failures so an undesirable event never happens.
notes.example: Like planning a journey around likely road works, but done step by step for a work process, such as a new booking system.
notes.source: CMS QAPI, Guidance for Performing Failure Mode and Effects Analysis with Performance Improvement Projects, “Overview”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is root cause analysis (RCA)?
notes.back: A structured way to deal with problems after they have happened.
notes.explanation: The nursing-home guide sets it beside FMEA: one looks back at a problem that has happened, the other looks ahead at failures that might.
notes.example: Like an accident investigation: the event has already occurred and the team works back to why.
notes.source: CMS QAPI, Guidance for Performing Failure Mode and Effects Analysis with Performance Improvement Projects, “Overview”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In FMEA, what does severity rate?
notes.back: How serious the consequence would be if the process failed in that way.
notes.explanation: The Department of Energy report rates every potential failure on three aspects: severity, occurrence and detection.
notes.example: A wrong label that could harm a patient rates higher than a smudged label that can still be read.
notes.source: US Department of Energy, FCIC Failure Mode and Effects Analysis Summary Report (FY22), DOE/EE-2734, “Introduction”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a risk priority number (RPN)?
notes.back: In FMEA, a score for each potential failure made by multiplying its severity, occurrence and detection ratings.
notes.explanation: The Department of Energy report says the team scores each potential failure this way so that failures can be ranked for action.
notes.example: Like a triage score, but built by multiplying three separate ratings for each way a process could fail.
notes.source: US Department of Energy, FCIC Failure Mode and Effects Analysis Summary Report (FY22), DOE/EE-2734, “Introduction”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does a clear pattern on a scatter plot prove that X causes Y?
notes.back: No. Causality implies association, but association does not imply causality.
notes.explanation: The e-Handbook: the plot shows structured association between X and Y, and that alone does not settle cause.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.3.26 “Scatter Plot”, “Causality Is Not Proved By Association”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: "Relationships" means that there is some structured association (linear, quadratic, etc.) between X and Y . Note, however, that even though causality implies association association does NOT imply causality.

notes.front: What range of values can Pearson's r take?
notes.back: From −1 to 1.
notes.explanation: At either end, a linear equation describes the relationship perfectly, with every point on a line.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Pearson correlation coefficient”, English Wikipedia, “Interpretation”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: The correlation coefficient ranges from −1 to 1. An absolute value of exactly 1 implies that a linear equation describes the relationship between X and Y perfectly, with all data points lying on a line .

notes.front: What do r = +1 and r = −1 each mean?
notes.back: +1: all points on a line where Y rises as X rises. −1: all points on a line where Y rises as X falls.
notes.explanation: The sign of r follows the sign of the regression slope, so it gives the direction of the relationship.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Pearson correlation coefficient”, English Wikipedia, “Interpretation”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: The correlation sign is determined by the regression slope : a value of +1 implies that all data points lie on a line for which Y increases as X increases, whereas a value of -1 implies a line where Y increases while X decreases.

notes.front: A Pearson's r of 0 implies that there is no {{c1::linear}} dependency between the variables.
notes.explanation: The coefficient measures linear correlation only, so a value of 0 speaks only about a straight-line link.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Pearson correlation coefficient”, English Wikipedia, “Interpretation”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: A value of 0 implies that there is no linear dependency between the variables.

notes.front: Why should you look at the scatter plot before trusting Pearson's r?
notes.back: r is not robust: its value can be misleading if outliers are present.
notes.explanation: r is neither distributionally robust nor outlier resistant, and the scatter plot will typically show when that matters.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Pearson correlation coefficient”, English Wikipedia, “Robustness”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: so its value can be misleading if outliers are present. [ 33 ] [ 34 ] Specifically, the PMCC is neither distributionally robust, [ 35 ] nor outlier resistant [ 32 ] (see Robust statistics §   Definition ). Inspection of the scatterplot between X and Y will typically reveal a situation where lack of robustness might be an issue

notes.front: In simple linear regression, the coefficient of determination is the {{c1::square}} of the sample correlation coefficient r.
notes.explanation: So a correlation of 0.9 gives r² = 0.81.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Coefficient of determination”, English Wikipedia
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: In simple linear regression (which includes an intercept ), r 2 is simply the square of the sample correlation coefficient ( r ), between the observed outcomes and the observed predictor values.

notes.front: In simple linear regression, how is the fitted slope related to r?
notes.back: Slope = r × s_y ÷ s_x: the correlation multiplied by the standard deviation of y divided by that of x.
notes.explanation: The intercept is then set so that the line passes through the centre of mass (x̄, ȳ) of the data.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Simple linear regression”, English Wikipedia
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: the slope of the fitted line is equal to the correlation between y and x corrected by the ratio of standard deviations of these variables. The intercept of the fitted line is such that the line passes through the center of mass ( x , y ) of the data points.

notes.front: What does the e-Handbook expect of a regression model's residuals?
notes.back: Roughly normal and roughly independent, with a mean of 0 and some constant variance.
notes.explanation: Residuals are the variation the fitted model leaves unexplained, a form of error, so the usual assumptions for errors apply.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 5.2.4 “Are the model residuals well-behaved?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Residuals can be thought of as elements of variation unexplained by the fitted model. Since this is a form of error, the same general assumptions apply to the group of residuals that we typically use for errors in general: one expects them to be (roughly) normal and (approximately) independently distributed with a mean of 0 and some constant variance .

notes.front: What does the e-Handbook call estimating a regression function outside the observed range of the predictors, and what does it advise?
notes.back: Extrapolation. It is sometimes necessary, but requires caution.
notes.explanation: Estimates inside the observed range are called interpolations; the e-Handbook singles out the outside ones for care.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 4.1.3 “What are process models used for?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Function values estimated for points within the observed space of predictor variable values are sometimes called interpolations. Estimation of regression function values for points outside the observed space of predictor variable values, called extrapolations, are sometimes necessary, but require caution.

notes.front: Can FMEA be used on a process that has not started yet?
notes.back: Yes. For a new process it can expose likely bottlenecks or unintended consequences before it is put in place.
notes.explanation: The nursing-home guide says FMEA works on both new and existing processes; on an existing one it shows how proposed changes would affect it.
notes.source: CMS QAPI, Guidance for Performing Failure Mode and Effects Analysis with Performance Improvement Projects, “When to use FMEA”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How are the bars on a Pareto chart ordered?
notes.back: In descending order of size or importance, from left to right.
notes.explanation: The guide ties this ordering to prioritising response actions.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional's Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 3: What Is Six Sigma?, “Pareto Charts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the Pareto principle, what are the “vital few” and the “trivial many”?
notes.back: Vital few: the few processes behind most quality problems. Trivial many: the many processes behind only a small share.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio puts the same idea as roughly 80% of the trouble coming from 20% of the problems.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional's Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 3: What Is Six Sigma?, “Pareto Charts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the seven-step FMEA guide for nursing homes, what is step 1?
notes.back: Select a process to analyse.
notes.explanation: The guide suggests a process known to be problem-prone, in the facility or in many facilities.
notes.source: CMS QAPI, Guidance for Performing Failure Mode and Effects Analysis with Performance Improvement Projects, steps overview, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the seven-step FMEA guide for nursing homes, what is step 2?
notes.back: Charter the project and select the team facilitator and team members.
notes.explanation: Leadership issues the charter and appoints the facilitator; members are people directly involved in the process.
notes.source: CMS QAPI, Guidance for Performing Failure Mode and Effects Analysis with Performance Improvement Projects, steps overview, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the seven-step FMEA guide for nursing homes, what is step 3?
notes.back: Describe the process.
notes.explanation: The guide asks the team to define the process steps clearly, because everyone must know exactly what is being analysed.
notes.source: CMS QAPI, Guidance for Performing Failure Mode and Effects Analysis with Performance Improvement Projects, steps overview, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the seven-step FMEA guide for nursing homes, what is step 4?
notes.back: Identify what could go wrong during each step of the process.
notes.explanation: People who work in the process list the problems that can or do occur at each step.
notes.source: CMS QAPI, Guidance for Performing Failure Mode and Effects Analysis with Performance Improvement Projects, steps overview, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the seven-step FMEA guide for nursing homes, what is step 5?
notes.back: Pick which problems to work on eliminating.
notes.explanation: The guide focuses on problems that happen often, have a serious impact when they do occur, or both.
notes.source: CMS QAPI, Guidance for Performing Failure Mode and Effects Analysis with Performance Improvement Projects, steps overview, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the seven-step FMEA guide for nursing homes, what is step 6?
notes.back: Design and implement changes to reduce or prevent the problems.
notes.explanation: The team decides how best to change the process so the risk of harm falls.
notes.source: CMS QAPI, Guidance for Performing Failure Mode and Effects Analysis with Performance Improvement Projects, steps overview, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the seven-step FMEA guide for nursing homes, what is step 7?
notes.back: Measure the success of the process changes.
notes.explanation: As in any improvement project, the team checks whether its changes worked.
notes.source: CMS QAPI, Guidance for Performing Failure Mode and Effects Analysis with Performance Improvement Projects, steps overview, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which two ratings does the nursing-home FMEA guide use to choose failures to work on, and what does it leave out that an RPN includes?
notes.back: Severity and probability of the failure; it has no detection rating.
notes.explanation: The Department of Energy report's RPN adds a third rating, detection, and multiplies all three.
notes.source: CMS QAPI, Guidance for Performing Failure Mode and Effects Analysis with Performance Improvement Projects, step 5, p. 6
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Risk priority number = severity × occurrence × {{c1::detection}}.
notes.explanation: Each failure gets three scores, and their product ranks it against the other failures.
notes.source: US Department of Energy, FCIC Failure Mode and Effects Analysis Summary Report (FY22), DOE/EE-2734, “Introduction”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In FMEA, what do the occurrence and detection ratings each measure?
notes.back: Occurrence: how often the failure is likely to happen. Detection: how easily it can be detected or prevented.
notes.explanation: Together with severity, they are the three aspects of a failure that make up the risk priority number.
notes.source: US Department of Energy, FCIC Failure Mode and Effects Analysis Summary Report (FY22), DOE/EE-2734, “Introduction”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which three types of FMEA does the Department of Energy report name?
notes.back: System FMEA, design FMEA and process FMEA.
notes.explanation: The report used the system type, because its aim was to improve the design of a whole system.
notes.source: US Department of Energy, FCIC Failure Mode and Effects Analysis Summary Report (FY22), DOE/EE-2734, “Introduction”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between an error and a residual?
notes.back: An error is measured from the true value (such as a population mean); a residual from an estimate (such as a sample mean).
notes.explanation: Wikipedia notes that the distinction is most important in regression analysis.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Errors and residuals”, English Wikipedia
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: The error of an observation is the deviation of the observed value from the true value of a quantity of interest (for example, a population mean ). The residual is the difference between the observed value and the estimated value of the quantity of interest (for example, a sample mean ). The distinction is most important in regression analysis

notes.front: A team finds r = −0.92 between the hours of operator training and the number of data-entry errors per week. What does this tell them?
notes.back: D) A strong linear relationship: as training rises, errors fall
notes.choices:
A) Almost no relationship, because the value is negative
B) Training causes errors to fall by 92%
C) The fitted line has a slope of −0.92
D) A strong linear relationship: as training rises, errors fall
notes.choicesExplained: A: a negative sign gives direction, not weakness. B: r measures association, not cause or percentage change. C: r does not give the slope.
notes.explanation: The sign gives direction and a value near −1 means the points lie close to a line.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Pearson correlation coefficient”, English Wikipedia, “Interpretation”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: The correlation sign is determined by the regression slope : a value of +1 implies that all data points lie on a line for which Y increases as X increases, whereas a value of -1 implies a line where Y increases while X decreases.

notes.front: In a simple linear regression of repair time on part weight, r = 0.7. About how much of the variance in repair time does weight explain?
notes.back: C) About 49%
notes.choices:
A) About 84%
B) About 70%
C) About 49%
D) About 30%
notes.choicesExplained: B: 70% treats r itself as the share explained. A: 84% is roughly the square root of 0.7, not its square. D: 30% is 1 − r, which has no such meaning.
notes.explanation: With one predictor, r² is the square of r and estimates the share of Y's variance explained by X: 0.7² = 0.49.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Pearson correlation coefficient”, English Wikipedia
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: The square of the sample correlation coefficient is typically denoted r 2 and is a special case of the coefficient of determination . In this case, it estimates the fraction of the variance in Y that is explained by X in a simple linear regression .

notes.front: Across twelve sites, hours of overtime correlate strongly with customer complaints (r = 0.85). A manager wants to cap overtime to cut complaints. What is the soundest response?
notes.back: A) Treat it as a lead: the correlation alone does not show that cutting overtime would reduce complaints
notes.choices:
A) Treat it as a lead: the correlation alone does not show that cutting overtime would reduce complaints
B) Ignore it: correlations between business measures are meaningless
C) Go ahead, but only at sites where r is also above 0.8
D) Go ahead: r above 0.8 shows overtime causes complaints
notes.choicesExplained: D: a high r shows association, not cause. B: correlations may give valuable clues to causal links. C: splitting by site still gives only correlation.
notes.explanation: A correlation can be a useful clue, but on its own it is not evidence that changing one variable would change the other.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Coefficient of determination”, English Wikipedia, “Caveats”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: while correlations may sometimes provide valuable clues in uncovering causal relationships among variables, a non-zero estimated correlation between two variables is not, on its own, evidence that changing the value of one variable would result in changes in the values of other variables.

notes.front: Four analysts propose ways to fit a straight line of cost against batch size. Which one describes the least-squares line?
notes.back: C) The line that makes the sum of squared vertical gaps from the points as small as possible
notes.choices:
A) The line joining the smallest and largest batch sizes
B) The line that passes through as many points exactly as it can
C) The line that makes the sum of squared vertical gaps from the points as small as possible
D) The line that makes the sum of the plain vertical gaps equal to zero
notes.choicesExplained: A: two points ignore the rest of the data. B: counting exact hits is not the least-squares criterion. D: gaps summing to zero is not the same as minimising squared gaps; many lines could do it.
notes.explanation: Least squares scores each candidate line by its squared residuals and keeps the one with the smallest total.
notes.source: Wikipedia contributors, “Simple linear regression”, English Wikipedia, “Fitting the regression line”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0
notes.evidence: in this article the "best" fit will be understood as in the least-squares approach: a line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals

notes.front: A plot of residuals against predicted cycle time shows tiny residuals for short cycles and ever larger ones for long cycles. What does the e-Handbook's guidance say about this?
notes.back: A) The model is suspect: the error level depends on the size of the prediction
notes.choices:
A) The model is suspect: the error level depends on the size of the prediction
B) The model is fine, because large cycles should have large errors
C) Nothing is wrong, as long as the residuals average zero
D) The residuals prove that the relationship is not linear
notes.choicesExplained: C: a zero mean is one assumption; constant variance is another. B: the e-Handbook wants the error level independent of the observation's size. D: a widening spread speaks to variance, not proof of curvature.
notes.explanation: The e-Handbook expects the size of the error to be independent of the size of the observation being predicted; here it grows with it.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 5.2.4 “Are the model residuals well-behaved?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: the level of the error should be independent of when the observation occurred in the study, or the size of the observation being predicted, or even the factor settings involved in making the prediction.

notes.front: A regression of dryer energy use was fitted on loads from 5 kg to 20 kg. The plant now wants a prediction for a 60 kg load. What does the e-Handbook advise?
notes.back: A) It is an extrapolation: possible, but use it with caution
notes.choices:
A) It is an extrapolation: possible, but use it with caution
B) It is an interpolation, so use it freely
C) Regression can never be used outside the data range
D) Refit the model with the 60 kg value set to the mean
notes.choicesExplained: B: 60 kg is outside the observed 5–20 kg range, so it is not an interpolation. C: the e-Handbook says extrapolations are sometimes necessary. D: inventing a data point does not make the estimate observed.
notes.explanation: Predictions outside the observed space of the predictors are extrapolations, which the e-Handbook says need caution.
notes.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 4.1.3 “What are process models used for?”
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain
notes.evidence: Estimation of regression function values for points outside the observed space of predictor variable values, called extrapolations, are sometimes necessary, but require caution.

notes.front: On a multi-vari chart of coating thickness, readings from Line 1 sit well above those from Line 2, while readings along a single panel and across the day barely change. Which family of variation dominates?
notes.back: D) Between machines or process parts
notes.choices:
A) Measurement error
B) Within a part
C) Over time
D) Between machines or process parts
notes.choicesExplained: B: readings along one panel barely change. C: readings across the day barely change. A: measurement error is not one of the three multi-vari families.
notes.explanation: LeanOhio's multi-vari splits variation into within a part, between machines or process parts, and over time.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Multi-vari”, p. 9
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which of these is best described as special cause variation?
notes.back: C) A jump in call wait times on the morning half the team was at a training course
notes.choices:
A) Small, random differences in call wait times from one hour to the next
B) The usual spread in how long agents take to type notes
C) A jump in call wait times on the morning half the team was at a training course
D) Minor day-to-day swings in call volume
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D are the ordinary, ever-present variation of the process, which is common cause variation.
notes.explanation: Special cause variation comes from an identifiable factor that knocks the output out of its normal random pattern.
notes.source: LeanOhio (Ohio Department of Administrative Services), Lean Six Sigma Terminology, ver. 2, “Special Cause Variation (Signals)”, p. 13
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A clinic gave a patient the wrong dose last week. The quality lead wants a structured look at why it happened. Which tool fits, according to the nursing-home FMEA guide?
notes.back: B) Root cause analysis
notes.choices:
A) FMEA, because it studies failures
B) Root cause analysis
C) A Pareto chart of this one event
D) A new process design before any analysis
notes.choicesExplained: A: FMEA looks for failures before they happen. C: a Pareto chart ranks many categories, not one event. D: the guide's tools analyse first.
notes.explanation: The guide separates the two by timing: after an event, root cause analysis; before one, FMEA.
notes.source: CMS QAPI, Guidance for Performing Failure Mode and Effects Analysis with Performance Improvement Projects, “Overview”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A payroll error is traced as: the payment was wrong because the rate was wrong; the rate was wrong because the form was out of date. The analyst stops there and reissues the form. What would the 5 Whys approach ask for?
notes.back: C) Keep asking why, such as why an out-of-date form was still in use, to reach a root cause
notes.choices:
A) Stop, because two answers are enough for a simple problem
B) Ask why the payment was wrong five more times
C) Keep asking why, such as why an out-of-date form was still in use, to reach a root cause
D) Start a Pareto chart of all payroll errors instead
notes.choicesExplained: A: the chain has stopped at a symptom, not a root cause. B: repeating the same question does not go deeper. D: a Pareto chart ranks problems; it does not trace this one's cause.
notes.explanation: The technique keeps asking “why?” until the chain reaches a root cause, not the first fixable symptom.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional's Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 3: What Is Six Sigma?, “5 Whys Approach”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A bakery's rolls vary because one flour supplier's deliveries differ in protein content. On a cause-and-effect diagram with six cause areas, which area holds this cause?
notes.back: Materials.
notes.explanation: The cause lies in what goes into the product, the supplied flour.

notes.front: A help desk logged 400 tickets: password resets 210, printer faults 90, software installs 60, network drops 25, other 15. The team can tackle only one category this quarter. Which tool shows most clearly where to start, and what would it show?
notes.back: A) A Pareto chart, with password resets as the first and tallest bar
notes.choices:
A) A Pareto chart, with password resets as the first and tallest bar
B) A cause-and-effect diagram, with printer faults at the head
C) A scatter plot of ticket count against category
D) A run chart of tickets in the order received
notes.choicesExplained: B: a cause-and-effect diagram explores causes of one effect; it does not rank categories. C: a scatter plot needs two measured variables, not categories. D: a run chart shows change over time, not which category is largest.
notes.explanation: Sorting the bars from largest to smallest puts the vital few categories first, which makes prioritising easier.
notes.source: US EPA, Environmental Professional's Guide to Lean and Six Sigma, Chapter 3: What Is Six Sigma?, “Pareto Charts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An FMEA team rates four failure modes (severity, occurrence, detection): mislabelled sample 8, 3, 3; late courier 6, 6, 6; power cut 10, 1, 6; typo in address 3, 8, 8. Using the risk priority number, which failure ranks first?
notes.back: A) Late courier (RPN 216)
notes.choices:
A) Late courier (RPN 216)
B) Typo in address (RPN 192)
C) Power cut, because it has the highest severity
D) Mislabelled sample (RPN 72)
notes.choicesExplained: C: severity alone is not the RPN; 10 × 1 × 6 = 60. B: 3 × 8 × 8 = 192, below 216. D: 8 × 3 × 3 = 72.
notes.explanation: RPN = severity × occurrence × detection: 72, 216, 60 and 192, so the late courier has the highest score.
notes.source: US Department of Energy, FCIC Failure Mode and Effects Analysis Summary Report (FY22), DOE/EE-2734, “Introduction”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team wants to find failures across a whole pre-processing plant made of several linked units, with special attention to the hand-offs between units. Which type of FMEA does the Department of Energy report describe for this?
notes.back: B) System FMEA
notes.choices:
A) Process FMEA
B) System FMEA
C) Design FMEA
D) Root cause analysis
notes.choicesExplained: A: the report names system FMEA, not process FMEA, as the highest-level analysis of a whole system. C: nor does it give that role to design FMEA. D: root cause analysis deals with problems after they occur.
notes.explanation: The report calls system FMEA the highest-level analysis, of a whole system made up of subsystems, including their interfaces.
notes.source: US Department of Energy, FCIC Failure Mode and Effects Analysis Summary Report (FY22), DOE/EE-2734, “Introduction”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On the Department of Energy report's scales, a failure has no process control that could catch it. Which detection rank should the team give it?
notes.choicesExplained: D: rank 1 means detection is almost certain. B: rank 3 is a high chance of detection. C: rank 6 is a moderate chance.
notes.explanation: Detection ranks rise as the chance of catching the failure falls, so no control at all takes the top rank.
notes.source: US Department of Energy, FCIC Failure Mode and Effects Analysis Summary Report (FY22), DOE/EE-2734, Table 3 “Detection guidance scale”, p. 3
